newsitem.title: USA: Clayton says plan for Kinko's like Lexmark plan.
newsitem.headline: Clayton says plan for Kinko's like Lexmark plan.

text.p: Clayton Dubilier & Rice Inc's co-president said the buyout firm's plan for Kinko's Inc is similar to its plan for Lexmark Holding Inc, the computer printer business it acquired from International Business Machines Corp in 1991 and brought public in 1995.

Kinko's and Clayton announced a key step in the process Thursday, the consolidation of all 130 Subchapter S corporations that operated under the Kinko's name into a single Delaware-based master corporation.

Concurrent with the "roll-up" of the disparate Kinko's entities, Clayton said it will invest about $214 million in Kinko's common stock through a Clayton-managed fund, a deal originally announced last June.

The investment makes Clayton Kinko's second largest shareholder with a stake in the "low-30s" percent while Kinko's founder and chairman Paul Orfalea remains the top holder with his "mid-30s percent" holding, according to Donald Gogel, Clayton co-president.
Also, Goldman Sachs acquired a "nominal" position in Kinko's after advising on the "roll-up," though Kinko's and Goldman spokesmen declined elaborate on the size.

Based in Ventura, Calif., and a fixture in nearly every U.S. college town, Kinko's provides office services, including document copying and binding and computer rentals, usually 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
The company was founded in 1970 by Orfalea near the University of California, Santa Barbara.
"There are 850 Kinko's stores now participating in five countries. We expect it to be a global entity with thousands of stores," Gogel said.

He noted that with aggressive international expansion, Kinko's intends to be in a dozen counties in the near future. Currently it operates in the Netherlands, Japan, South Korea, Canada and United States.

Lexmark, IBM's former printer division with roots in the Selectric typewriter, was acquired by Clayton for $1.5 billion. Clayton still holds 30 percent of the company. In November of 1995, Goldman led an initial public offering of 17.1 million shares at $20 each.
Lexmark shares were off 1-1/2 to 26-1/8 in New York Stock Exchange trade Thursday, near the year-high 27-1/4.
